options: The route/altitude prescribed by the lost-communications procedure
Any direct route at any altitude
An immediate descent to the surface
questions.explain: Lost-comms rules specify the route (assigned/expected/filed) and altitude (highest of assigned/minimum/expected) to fly, and the transponder code 7600.

questions.q: An IFR flight plan must generally include —
options: Route, altitude, ETE, fuel, alternate (as required) and aircraft data
questions.explain: An IFR flight plan carries route, altitudes, timings, fuel, alternate and aircraft/equipment details.

questions.q: An alternate aerodrome must be planned for an IFR flight when —
options: Destination weather is forecast below prescribed minima for the required period
questions.explain: Rules require filing an alternate when the destination forecast within the specified window is below the prescribed ceiling/visibility.

questions.q: The transponder code to squawk for an IFR flight, unless assigned otherwise, is —
questions.explain: IFR flights squawk the discrete code ATC assigns (VFR conskpicuity codes like 1200/7000 are for VFR).

questions.q: Required IFR equipment includes navigation gear appropriate to the route plus —
options: Two-way radio communications and the instruments for instrument flight
questions.explain: IFR requires the instruments/equipment for instrument flight and two-way radio and navigation equipment appropriate to the ground facilities used.

questions.q: A 'cruise' clearance to an airport authorises the pilot to —
options: Conduct the flight at any altitude from the minimum IFR altitude up to the assigned, and to make an approach
questions.explain: A cruise clearance lets the pilot fly at any altitude between the minimum IFR altitude and the assigned altitude and to commence an approach at the destination.

questions.q: Position reports on an IFR flight (in a non-radar environment) are made —
questions.explain: In non-radar airspace, IFR position reports are made over compulsory reporting points.

questions.q: Class A airspace requires operation —
questions.explain: All operations in Class A airspace are conducted under IFR with an ATC clearance.

banks.title: Instrument Procedures
banks.desc: Approaches, holding and instrument procedures (GACAR Part 97 and the Saudi AIP ENR).
banks.source: GACAR Part 97 · Saudi AIP (ENR) · DRAFT — pending review

questions.q: GACAR Part 97 exists primarily to —
options: Identify the approved instrument flight procedures (IFPs) authorized for use in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
questions.explain: §97.1 states that Part 97 identifies the approved instrument flight procedures (including instrument approach procedures) authorized for use within the territorial limits of the KSA.

questions.q: Under GACAR §97.1, the rules governing the development, validation and approval of instrument flight procedures are addressed under —
questions.explain: §97.1(d) provides that development, validation, approval, promulgation and maintenance of IFPs are addressed under GACAR Part 172, not within Part 97.

questions.q: Per GACAR §97.1, the publication of instrument flight procedures in the KSA AIP and their depiction on aeronautical charts are governed by —
questions.explain: §97.1(e) states the rules for publishing IFPs in the KSA AIP and depicting them on charts are addressed under GACAR Part 175.

questions.q: Under GACAR §97.3, an aircraft approach category is a grouping based on a speed of —
options: Vref (or 1.3 Vso if Vref is not specified) at the maximum certificated landing mass
Vso at the maximum takeoff mass
V2 at the maximum landing mass
questions.explain: §97.3(a) defines the aircraft approach category by a speed of Vref, or, if Vref is not specified, 1.3 Vso at the maximum certificated landing mass.

questions.q: Under the aircraft approach categories in GACAR §97.3, Category A applies to a speed of —
questions.explain: §97.3(a)(1) assigns Category A to aircraft with an approach speed of less than 91 knots indicated airspeed.

questions.q: Under GACAR §97.3, aircraft approach Category C covers a speed of —
options: 166 knots IAS or more but less than 211 knots IAS
questions.explain: §97.3(a)(3) defines Category C as 121 knots or more but less than 141 knots IAS.

questions.q: Per the approach segment definitions in GACAR §97.3, the initial approach segment lies between the initial approach fix and —
options: The intermediate fix (or the point where the aircraft is established on the intermediate course/final approach course)
questions.explain: §97.3(c)(1) defines the initial approach segment as running from the initial approach fix to the intermediate fix, or to where the aircraft is established on the intermediate or final approach course.

questions.q: In GACAR §97.3, the final approach segment of an instrument approach procedure is the segment in which —
options: The aircraft climbs after a missed approach
Alignment and descent for landing are accomplished
The aircraft is vectored to the initial approach fix
questions.explain: §97.3(c)(4) describes the final approach segment as the segment in which alignment and descent for landing are accomplished.

questions.q: According to GACAR §97.3, the missed approach segment of an instrument approach procedure starts at the —
questions.explain: §97.3(c)(5) states the missed approach segment starts at the missed approach point and comprises an initial, intermediate and final phase.

questions.q: Under GACAR §97.3, the intermediate phase of the missed approach extends from the start of climb to the point where obstacle clearance of at least — is first obtained and can be maintained.
questions.explain: §97.3(c)(5)(ii) defines the intermediate phase as extending from the start of climb to where 50 m (164 ft) of obstacle clearance is first obtained and can be maintained.

questions.q: Per GACAR §97.3, a procedure turn is a maneuver in which a turn is made away from a designated track followed by a turn in the opposite direction to —
options: Enter a holding pattern at the fix
Permit the aircraft to intercept and proceed along the reciprocal of the designated track
Establish the aircraft on the missed approach
questions.explain: §97.3(d) defines a procedure turn as a turn away from a designated track and then a turn in the opposite direction so the aircraft can intercept and proceed along the reciprocal of that track.

questions.q: Under GACAR §97.5, all bearings, courses, tracks, headings and radials in the instrument procedures of Part 97 are expressed in —
questions.explain: §97.5(a) provides that all bearings, courses, tracks, headings and radials in Part 97 are in degrees magnetic unless otherwise designated.

questions.q: In the instrument procedures of GACAR Part 97, runway visual range (RVR) values are stated in —
questions.explain: §97.5(b) states RVR values are stated in meters, while other mileages are stated in nautical miles or applicable SI units.

questions.q: Under GACAR §97.11, approved IFPs (including instrument approach and departure procedures) in the KSA are developed and maintained by —
options: Air navigation service providers certificated under GACAR Part 170 providing IFP services under Part 172
questions.explain: §97.11(a) provides that approved IFPs are developed and maintained by air navigation service providers certificated under GACAR Part 170 and providing instrument flight procedure services under GACAR Part 172.

questions.q: According to the Saudi AIP, the transition level (TL) for the whole JEDDAH FIR has been fixed by GACA at —
questions.explain: Saudi AIP ENR 1.1 (Transition level) states the TL has been determined by GACA as fixed at FL 150 for the whole of JEDDAH FIR.

questions.q: Per the Saudi AIP, the fixed transition level of FL 150 in JEDDAH FIR is also described as the —
options: Standard cruising level for all IFR flights
questions.explain: Saudi AIP ENR 1.1 notes that the transition level, fixed at FL 150, is therefore also the lowest usable flight level for the JEDDAH FIR.

questions.q: Under the Saudi AIP cruising-level rules, en-route cruising levels are expressed in flight levels at and above —
questions.explain: Saudi AIP ENR 1.1 (Cruising levels) states levels are expressed as altitude at and below 13,000 FT AMSL, or as flight level at and above FL 150.

questions.q: Per the Saudi AIP, the appropriate flight information service (FIS) frequency for an aerodrome is published —
options: Only in the GEN section of the AIP
At the top of all instrument approach charts
On the en-route chart margins only
questions.explain: Saudi AIP ENR 1.1 notes that the appropriate FIS frequency is published at the top of all instrument approach charts.

questions.q: Per the Saudi AIP, a pilot who has not received a landing clearance approaching short final shall —
options: Continue and land, then advise the tower
Request a landing clearance, and if not in receipt of one commence a missed approach not later than the runway landing threshold
Enter a holding pattern over the threshold
Reduce to minimum speed and orbit on final
questions.explain: Saudi AIP ENR 1.1 states a landing clearance shall be requested approaching short final, and pilots not in receipt of one shall commence a missed approach not later than the runway landing threshold.

questions.q: Under the Saudi AIP general speed limits, aircraft operated below ALT 10,000 FT anywhere in JEDDAH FIR must not exceed an indicated airspeed of —
questions.explain: Saudi AIP ENR 1.1 (Speed limits) sets a maximum of 250 KT IAS below 10,000 FT elsewhere in the FIR (with a lower limit inside the aerodrome traffic circuit).

questions.q: Per the Saudi AIP, the highest altitude at which a VFR flight may operate within JEDDAH FIR is —
questions.explain: Saudi AIP ENR 1.2 (Maximum level for VFR) states the highest altitude at which a VFR flight may operate within JEDDAH FIR is 12,500 FT.

questions.q: Per the Saudi AIP, an aircraft joining the aerodrome traffic circuit from the same side as the traffic pattern shall normally —
options: Join straight in on the base leg
Arrange flight to join straight in on the downwind leg
Overfly the aerodrome at circuit height then join crosswind
questions.explain: Saudi AIP ENR 1.1 states aircraft approaching from the same side as the traffic pattern shall arrange flight to join straight in on the downwind leg (those from the opposite side cross over the aerodrome at midfield first).

questions.q: A published instrument approach procedure's final approach segment ends at —
options: The missed approach point (or runway threshold on a precision approach)
questions.explain: The final approach segment runs from the final approach fix to the missed approach point (or, on an ILS, to the DA/threshold), where a missed approach is flown if not visual.

questions.q: A standard holding pattern uses —
options: Right turns with the timing/leg length specified for the altitude
questions.explain: The standard hold uses right-hand turns; inbound leg timing (commonly 1 minute at or below 14,000 ft, 1.5 minutes above) or a DME/RNAV distance defines the pattern.

questions.q: On a precision (ILS) approach, reaching the Decision Altitude/Height without the required visual reference requires the pilot to —
options: Enter a hold on the localiser
questions.explain: At DA/DH, if the required visual references are not in sight, the pilot must initiate the published missed approach.

questions.q: The three ICAO instrument-approach segments preceding the missed approach are —
questions.explain: An instrument approach is built from the initial, intermediate and final approach segments (with the missed approach as the fourth), each with its own obstacle-clearance criteria.

questions.q: A standard instrument approach procedure is designed to provide —
options: A safe transition from the en-route/terminal phase to a landing (or missed approach)
questions.explain: An instrument approach procedure provides obstacle-protected guidance from the initial approach to landing or the missed approach.

questions.q: A precision approach provides —
questions.explain: Precision approaches (ILS, GLS, PAR) give both lateral and vertical guidance; non-precision give lateral only (with possible advisory vertical).

questions.q: The decision altitude/height (DA/DH) on a precision approach is the point at which —
options: A missed approach must be started if the required visual reference is not available
questions.explain: At DA/DH, without the required visual reference, the missed approach is initiated.

questions.q: A procedure turn is used to —
options: Reverse course and establish the aircraft inbound on the final approach course
questions.explain: The procedure turn reverses direction to align the aircraft with the final approach course when required.

questions.q: The final approach segment of a non-precision approach ends at the —
questions.explain: The non-precision final approach segment runs from the FAF to the MAPt.

questions.q: A STAR (standard terminal arrival) connects —
options: The en-route structure to an approach fix
questions.explain: STARs provide a published transition from the en-route phase to the approach.

questions.q: Holding pattern entries (direct, parallel, teardrop) are chosen based on —
options: The aircraft's heading relative to the holding course on arrival
questions.explain: The entry (direct/parallel/teardrop) is selected from the aircraft's inbound heading relative to the holding course.

questions.q: A missed approach is executed by —
options: Following the published missed-approach procedure (climb, track, hold)
questions.explain: The published missed approach specifies the climb, track and clearance limit/holding to fly when a landing is not made.

questions.q: Circling to land after an instrument approach requires the pilot to —
options: Remain within the protected circling area at or above circling minima until aligned to land
questions.explain: During a circling manoeuvre the aircraft stays within the protected area at/above circling MDA until in a position to descend to land.

questions.q: On the Saudi AIP ENR pages, en-route ATS routes and their minimum altitudes are found in —
questions.explain: The ENR part of the AIP publishes ATS routes, airspace and en-route procedures.

questions.q: Descent below the MDA/DA on an approach is permitted only when —
options: The required visual reference and flight visibility exist and a normal landing can be made
questions.explain: Descent below minima requires the specified visual references, the required visibility, and the aircraft in a position for a normal landing.

questions.q: A DME arc procedure is used to —
options: Join the final approach course at a constant distance from a station
questions.explain: A DME arc guides the aircraft at a fixed DME distance to intercept the final approach course.

banks.title: Instrument Rating Requirements
banks.desc: Eligibility, experience and currency for the instrument rating under GACAR Part 61.
banks.source: GACAR Part 61 (Instrument Rating) · DRAFT — pending review

questions.q: Under GACAR Part 61, to apply for an instrument rating a person must, at minimum —
options: Hold at least a current private pilot certificate (or be concurrently applying for one) with an appropriate aircraft rating
Hold only a student pilot certificate
questions.explain: GACAR §61.89(a)(1) requires an instrument-rating applicant to hold at least a current private pilot certificate — or be concurrently applying for one — with an airplane, helicopter, or powered-lift rating appropriate to the instrument rating sought.

questions.q: Under §61.89, an instrument-rating applicant who does not already hold one must pass a knowledge test on the aeronautical knowledge areas of —
questions.explain: GACAR §61.89(a)(2) requires the applicant (unless already instrument-rated) to pass the knowledge test on the aeronautical knowledge areas of Appendix B to GACAR Part 141.

questions.q: Under §61.89, no person may act as PIC of a civil aircraft under IFR, or in weather less than the minimums for VFR flight, unless that person holds —
options: An appropriate category/class/type rating and an instrument rating (or equivalent ATP privileges)
questions.explain: GACAR §61.89(b) bars acting as PIC under IFR or in below-VFR weather unless the pilot holds the appropriate category, class, and type rating plus an instrument rating for the aircraft (or the equivalent ATP privileges).

questions.q: To act as PIC under IFR, §61.17 requires that within the preceding period the pilot have performed and logged, among other tasks, at least —
questions.explain: GACAR §61.17(a)(3) requires, for instrument recent experience, at least six instrument approaches (plus holding procedures and course tracking) performed solely by reference to instruments.

questions.q: Under §61.17, the instrument approaches, holding, and course-tracking tasks required to act as PIC under IFR (in an aircraft) must have been performed within the preceding —
questions.explain: GACAR §61.17(a)(3)(i) sets the instrument recent-experience window at the 6 months preceding the month of the flight.

questions.q: Which task is part of the instrument recent experience §61.17 requires to act as PIC under IFR?
options: Intercepting and tracking courses using electronic navigation systems
A biennial flight review in a glider
questions.explain: GACAR §61.17(a)(3) lists intercepting and tracking courses using electronic navigation systems (along with six instrument approaches and holding procedures) as an instrument recent-experience task.

questions.q: Under §61.17, a pilot who has not met the instrument experience requirements for more than six calendar months may regain instrument currency only by —
questions.explain: GACAR §61.17(a)(4) provides that once the instrument experience lapse exceeds six calendar months, currency can be reestablished only by completing an instrument proficiency check.

questions.q: Under §61.17, an instrument proficiency check must consist of —
options: The areas of operation and instrument tasks required in the instrument rating practical test standards
A short oral quiz on weather theory
The night takeoff and landing recency tasks
questions.explain: GACAR §61.17(a)(4) states the instrument proficiency check must consist of the areas of operation and instrument tasks required in the instrument rating practical test standards.

questions.q: Under §61.17, an instrument proficiency check may be given by all of the following EXCEPT —
options: Any private pilot who happens to hold an instrument rating
An authorized company check pilot under GACAR Part 121, 125, or 135
questions.explain: GACAR §61.17(a)(4)(ii) lists who may give the check — an examiner, an authorized instructor, an authorized company check pilot, or a person approved by the President — but not simply any instrument-rated private pilot.

questions.q: Under §61.89, if instrument-rating privileges are to be exercised in multi-engine aircraft, the flight training must include operating the aircraft solely by reference to instruments —
questions.explain: GACAR §61.89(c) requires that multi-engine instrument training include operating the aircraft of the appropriate category solely by reference to instruments with one engine inoperative.

questions.q: Under §61.89, a person holding or applying for an instrument rating on a private pilot certificate must hold a Class 1 medical certificate or —
options: Obtain a waiver from the President
Have established hearing acuity meeting the Class 1 medical hearing requirements
questions.explain: GACAR §61.89(d) requires either a Class 1 medical certificate or established hearing acuity based on compliance with the hearing requirements for issue of a Class 1 medical certificate.

questions.q: Under §61.89, to act as PIC of a glider under IFR a person must hold a pilot certificate with a glider category rating and —
questions.explain: GACAR §61.89(b)(3) allows a glider to be flown under IFR by a person holding a pilot certificate with a glider category rating and an airplane instrument rating.

questions.q: Under §61.19, a person may serve as SIC of an aircraft under IFR only if, among other requirements, that person holds —
options: An instrument rating or privilege applicable to the aircraft being flown
A type rating in every aircraft in the fleet
questions.explain: GACAR §61.19(a)(2) requires an SIC to hold an instrument rating, or privilege applicable to the aircraft being flown, when the flight is conducted under IFR.

questions.q: Under §61.89, an instrument-rating applicant must pass a practical test on the areas of operation prescribed in —
questions.explain: GACAR §61.89(a)(4) requires the applicant to pass the practical test on the areas of operation set out in Appendix B to GACAR Part 141.

questions.q: Under §61.17, when instrument recent experience is accomplished in an aviation training device (ATD), the required tasks must have been performed within the preceding —
questions.explain: GACAR §61.17(a)(3) provides a shorter window for ATD-based instrument recency: the required tasks (including 3 hours and six approaches) must be within the 2 months preceding the month of the flight.

questions.q: Under §61.89, which is an acceptable way to meet the instrument-rating training requirement?
options: Simply holding a valid medical certificate
Graduating from an approved instrument rating course under Appendix B to GACAR Part 141
questions.explain: GACAR §61.89(a)(3) lists acceptable training routes, including a certificate of graduation from an approved instrument rating certification course under Appendix B to GACAR Part 141.

questions.q: The instrument recent-experience tasks in §61.17 must be performed —
options: Solely by reference to instruments, in actual or simulated instrument flight conditions
Only in actual IMC with a safety pilot
Only in a full flight simulator
questions.explain: GACAR §61.17(a)(3) requires the recent-experience tasks to be performed solely by reference to instruments, in actual or simulated instrument flight conditions.

questions.q: Under GACAR Part 61, an instrument rating is required in order to —
options: Carry passengers for hire in day VFR
Act as PIC under IFR or in weather below the minimums for VFR flight
Fly a single-engine airplane in day VFR
questions.explain: GACAR §61.89(b) makes an instrument rating a prerequisite to acting as PIC under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR flight.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the recent-experience tasks §61.17 requires to act as PIC under IFR?
options: A power-off stall series in VMC
questions.explain: GACAR §61.17(a)(3) lists holding procedures and tasks, along with six instrument approaches and course tracking, as instrument recent-experience requirements.

questions.q: Under §61.17, an instrument proficiency check (for other than a glider) may be conducted in an aircraft appropriate to the category or in —
options: An FSTD representative of the aircraft category
questions.explain: GACAR §61.17(a)(4)(i) allows the instrument proficiency check to be conducted in an aircraft appropriate to the category or, for other than a glider, in an FSTD that is representative of the aircraft category.

questions.q: Under §61.89, an applicant for an instrument rating who does not yet hold a private pilot certificate may —
options: Apply for the instrument rating concurrently with the private pilot certificate
Never be issued an instrument rating
Skip the private pilot requirement entirely
Obtain it only after logging 1,500 hours
questions.explain: GACAR §61.89(a)(1) permits an applicant to be concurrently applying for the private pilot certificate (with the appropriate aircraft rating) while seeking the instrument rating.

questions.q: An instrument rating permits a pilot to —
options: Operate under IFR and in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC)
questions.explain: The instrument rating authorises flight under IFR and in IMC, within the privileges of the underlying pilot certificate.

questions.q: Instrument-rating aeronautical experience emphasises —
options: Instrument flight time, including cross-country under IFR and instrument approaches
questions.explain: The rating requires prescribed instrument time — actual or simulated — including cross-country IFR flying and a number of instrument approaches.

questions.q: To act as PIC under IFR, a pilot must, in addition to holding an instrument rating, be —
options: Instrument current (recent instrument experience within the required period)
questions.explain: IFR PIC privileges require instrument currency — the prescribed recent instrument experience (approaches, holding and tracking) within the look-back period.

questions.q: An instrument-rating applicant must pass —
options: An instrument knowledge test and an instrument practical test
questions.explain: The instrument rating requires passing both the instrument aeronautical-knowledge test and the instrument practical (flight) test.

questions.q: An instrument rating authorises flight —
options: Under IFR and in instrument meteorological conditions
questions.explain: The instrument rating permits operating under IFR/in IMC in the appropriate category.

questions.q: An instrument-rating applicant must demonstrate proficiency in —
options: Control and navigation of the aircraft solely by reference to instruments
questions.explain: The rating tests instrument flying — attitude instrument flying, holding, approaches — by reference to instruments alone.

questions.q: Instrument currency (to act as PIC under IFR) typically requires recent —
options: Approaches, holding and course tracking within the recency period
questions.explain: IFR recency requires a specified number of instrument approaches plus holding and intercepting/tracking tasks within the preceding period.

questions.q: If instrument currency lapses, the pilot regains it by —
options: An instrument proficiency check (IPC) after the grace period expires
questions.explain: After the currency window (and grace period) lapses, an instrument proficiency check is required to resume IFR PIC privileges.

questions.q: A required instrument-rating knowledge area is —
options: IFR procedures, the ATC system, and instrument approach charts
questions.explain: Instrument knowledge covers the ATC/IFR system, procedures, charts, weather and instrument navigation.

questions.q: Instrument experience must generally include —
options: Cross-country flight under IFR and instrument flight time
Only simulator time with no flight
questions.explain: The rating requires instrument flight time and IFR cross-country experience, part of which may be in an approved training device.

questions.q: A safety pilot is required when a pilot practises instrument flying —
options: Under simulated instrument conditions (a view-limiting device) in VMC
questions.explain: Simulated instrument flight (hood/foggles) in VMC requires an appropriately rated safety pilot with adequate vision and controls.

questions.q: The instrument rating is added to a pilot certificate as —
options: A rating on the existing certificate
A separate licence with a new number
questions.explain: The instrument rating is an additional rating placed on the pilot certificate.

questions.q: Attitude instrument flying relies primarily on the —
options: Attitude indicator supported by the supporting/performance instruments
questions.explain: The control-and-performance (or primary-and-supporting) method centres on the attitude indicator, cross-checked with the other instruments.

questions.q: An instrument-rated pilot filing IFR must ensure the aircraft is —
options: Equipped and certified for IFR with current inspections (e.g. pitot-static, transponder)
questions.explain: IFR requires the aircraft to be IFR-equipped and to have the required current inspections (pitot-static/altimeter, transponder, VOR checks as applicable).

questions.q: The instrument proficiency check must be given by —
questions.explain: An IPC is conducted by an authorised instructor/examiner and covers the required instrument tasks.

questions.q: A pilot without a current medical may not —
options: Exercise instrument PIC privileges requiring that medical
questions.explain: Exercising IFR PIC privileges still requires the appropriate valid medical certificate.

questions.q: Intercepting and tracking a course using navigation systems is —
questions.explain: Intercepting and tracking courses/radials/GPS paths is a fundamental instrument competency.

banks.title: Airline Transport Pilot Licensing
banks.desc: ATP certificate eligibility, aeronautical experience, privileges and limitations (GACAR Part 61, Subpart G).
banks.source: GACAR Part 61, Subpart G · DRAFT — pending review

questions.q: Which pilot certificate is governed by GACAR Part 61, Subpart G?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.171 states that Subpart G prescribes the requirements for the issuance of airline transport pilot (ATP) certificates and ratings, the conditions under which they are necessary, and their privileges and limitations.

questions.q: Under GACAR Part 61, the minimum age to be eligible for an airline transport pilot (ATP) certificate is —
questions.explain: GACAR §61.173(a) requires an ATP certificate applicant to be at least 23 years of age.

questions.q: Which class of medical certificate must an applicant generally hold to exercise the privileges of an ATP certificate?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.173(i) requires an ATP applicant to hold a Class 1 medical certificate (with a limited glider/balloon exception permitting a Class 2).

questions.q: For an ATP certificate with an airplane category and class rating, what is the minimum total time as a pilot required?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.181(a) requires at least 1,500 hours of total time as a pilot for an ATP certificate with an airplane category and class rating.

questions.q: The aeronautical experience for an ATP airplane rating must include at least how many hours of cross-country flight time?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.181(a)(1) requires at least 500 hours of cross-country flight time within the 1,500-hour total for an ATP airplane rating.

questions.q: How many hours of night flight time are required for an ATP certificate with an airplane category and class rating?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.181(a)(2) requires at least 100 hours of night flight time for an ATP airplane rating.

questions.q: The ATP airplane aeronautical experience requirement includes at least how many hours of instrument flight time in actual or simulated instrument conditions?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.181(a)(4) requires at least 75 hours of instrument flight time in actual or simulated instrument conditions for an ATP airplane rating.

questions.q: For an ATP airplane rating, at least how many hours of flight time must be as pilot in command (or as SIC performing PIC duties under supervision)?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.181(a)(5) requires at least 250 hours of flight time in an airplane as PIC, or as SIC performing the duties of a PIC under supervision, for an ATP airplane rating.

questions.q: For an ATP certificate with a rotorcraft category and helicopter class rating, what is the minimum total time as a pilot required?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.183(a) requires at least 1,200 hours of total time as a pilot for an ATP certificate with a rotorcraft category and helicopter class rating.

questions.q: For an ATP certificate with a powered-lift category rating, what is the minimum total time as a pilot required?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.185(a) requires at least 1,500 hours of total time as a pilot for an ATP certificate with a powered-lift category rating.

questions.q: In multi-pilot international operations under GACAR Part 121 or 135, a pilot holding an ATP certificate may not serve as a pilot after attaining which birthday?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.3(c) bars a commercial or ATP certificate holder from serving as a pilot in international Part 121/135 operations after the 60th birthday, or the 65th birthday in the case of operations with more than one pilot.

questions.q: Under GACAR §61.175, when is an applicant NOT required to pass a knowledge test to add an aircraft type rating to an ATP certificate?
options: When the ATP certificate already lists the aircraft category and class rating appropriate to the type rating sought
Never — a knowledge test is always required
When the applicant is over 40 years of age
When the applicant holds a foreign private pilot licence
questions.explain: GACAR §61.175(b) waives the knowledge test for an additional aircraft type rating when the applicant's ATP certificate already lists the aircraft category and class rating appropriate to the type rating sought.

questions.q: The ATP certification training program for an airplane multiengine class rating requires at least how many hours of academic (classroom) instruction?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.177(a) requires at least 30 hours of classroom instruction in the ATP certification training program for an airplane multiengine class rating.

questions.q: Within the ATP certification training program (airplane multiengine), how many hours of flight-simulation training device (FSTD) training are required?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.177(b) requires at least 10 hours of training in an FSTD representing a multiengine turbine airplane as part of the ATP certification training program.

questions.q: For an ATP airplane rating, at least how many hours must be flown in the specific class of airplane for the rating sought?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.181(a)(3) requires at least 50 hours of flight time in the class of airplane for the rating sought (with limited FFS credit).

questions.q: For an ATP rotorcraft/helicopter rating, the 100 hours of required night flight time must include at least how many hours in helicopters?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.183(a)(2) requires 100 hours of night flight time, of which at least 15 hours are in helicopters, for an ATP rotorcraft/helicopter rating.

questions.q: Which of the following is a valid eligibility path to an ATP certificate under GACAR §61.173?
options: Holding a commercial pilot certificate with an instrument rating
Holding a private pilot certificate only
questions.explain: GACAR §61.173(c) requires the applicant to hold a commercial pilot certificate with an instrument rating (or a qualifying foreign ATP licence with instrument privileges).

questions.q: For an ATP rotorcraft/helicopter rating, at least how many hours of cross-country flight time are required?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.183(a)(1) requires at least 500 hours of cross-country flight time for an ATP certificate with a rotorcraft category and helicopter class rating.

questions.q: For an ATP powered-lift rating, at least how many hours must be flown in a powered-lift as PIC (or as SIC performing PIC duties under supervision)?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.185(a)(3) requires at least 250 hours in a powered-lift as PIC, or as SIC performing the duties of a PIC under supervision, for an ATP powered-lift rating.

questions.q: For the ATP airplane rating, not more than how many hours of the total aeronautical experience may be obtained in a full flight simulator or flight training device (in an approved course)?
questions.explain: GACAR §61.181(a)(6) allows not more than 100 hours of the total aeronautical experience to be obtained in a full flight simulator or flight training device representing an airplane, when accomplished in an approved Part 121/135/141/142 course.

questions.q: Besides the minimum age, which is an eligibility requirement for an ATP certificate under GACAR §61.173?
options: Be currently employed by an airline
questions.explain: GACAR §61.173(b) requires an ATP certificate applicant to be of good moral character, in addition to the age and other requirements.

questions.q: To be eligible for an ATP certificate with an airplane multiengine class rating, GACAR §61.173(d) requires the applicant to present —
options: A graduation certificate for the ATP certification training program (§61.177)
A university degree in aeronautical engineering
A type rating in a widebody aircraft
questions.explain: GACAR §61.173(d) requires, for an airplane multiengine class ATP rating, a graduation certificate from an authorized training provider certifying completion of the ATP certification training program specified in §61.177 before taking the knowledge test.

questions.q: The ATP certificate is the —
options: Highest level of pilot certificate, required to act as PIC of scheduled air-carrier aircraft
questions.explain: The Airline Transport Pilot certificate is the highest pilot certificate and is required to act as PIC (and, per the rules, SIC) of certain air-carrier operations.

questions.q: A defining ATP eligibility requirement, compared with the commercial certificate, is —
options: A higher minimum age (typically 21) and substantially greater flight experience
questions.explain: ATP applicants must meet a higher minimum age (generally 21) and far greater aeronautical experience, including significant PIC and cross-country/night time.

questions.q: An ATP applicant must hold at least —
options: A commercial pilot certificate with an instrument rating (or equivalent)
questions.explain: ATP certification builds on a commercial certificate with an instrument rating (or an acceptable equivalent), plus the additional experience and testing.

questions.q: An ATP certificate holder must hold a medical certificate of at least —
options: Class 1 for the relevant airline-transport privileges
questions.explain: Exercising airline-transport (air carrier PIC) privileges requires the highest, Class 1, medical certificate.

questions.q: The airline transport pilot certificate is the —
questions.explain: The ATP is the highest pilot certificate, required for airline captain (and, as specified, first-officer) duties.

questions.q: The minimum age for an ATP certificate is —
questions.explain: An ATP applicant must be at least 21 years of age.

questions.q: An ATP applicant must hold —
questions.explain: ATP privileges require a Class 1 medical certificate.

questions.q: The ATP requires substantial aeronautical experience, typically on the order of —
options: Around 1,500 hours total time (with specified components)
questions.explain: The ATP demands large totals — on the order of 1,500 hours including cross-country, night, instrument and PIC components.

questions.q: To act as PIC of a large transport aircraft, in addition to the ATP a pilot needs —
options: A type rating for that aircraft
questions.explain: A type rating for the specific transport aircraft is required alongside the ATP.

questions.q: An ATP holder must maintain competence through —
options: Recurrent training, checks and currency requirements
questions.explain: Airline crews undergo recurrent training and proficiency/line checks to retain qualification.

questions.q: The ATP knowledge test covers advanced subjects including —
options: Air-transport operations, meteorology, performance and crew resource management
questions.explain: ATP knowledge spans advanced meteorology, transport performance, operations, navigation and human factors/CRM.

questions.q: An ATP practical test is conducted to —
questions.explain: The ATP practical test applies the highest airman proficiency standards.

questions.q: Crew resource management (CRM) training for airline crews aims to improve —
options: Communication, workload management and decision-making in the crew
questions.explain: CRM develops effective use of all resources — people, information and equipment — to reduce error.

questions.q: A first officer at an airline must, at minimum, hold —
options: The certificate/qualifications required by the operating rules (often ATP or as specified) and a type rating as applicable
questions.explain: Required flight-crew qualifications are set by the operating rules; airline pilots hold the ATP (or the specified certificate) and the appropriate type rating.

questions.q: An ATP certificate does not exempt the holder from —
questions.explain: Even ATP holders must meet recency, medical and type-rating currency requirements to exercise privileges.

questions.q: The high experience requirement for the ATP exists to ensure —
options: A demonstrated depth of skill and judgement for air-transport command
questions.explain: The ATP's experience thresholds are intended to ensure the maturity and skill appropriate to airline command.

banks.title: Air Transport Operations
banks.desc: Operating rules for transport-category commercial air operators under GACAR Part 121.

questions.q: GACAR Part 121 prescribes rules governing the scheduled and unscheduled operations of a commercial air operator operating which category of aircraft?
options: Transport category airplanes/rotorcraft or commuter category airplanes
questions.explain: GACAR §121.1 applies Part 121 to commercial air operators operating transport category airplanes, transport category rotorcraft, or commuter category airplanes that hold or must hold an Air Operator Certificate.

questions.q: Under GACAR Part 121, a certificate holder must hold or be required to hold an Air Operator Certificate (AOC) issued under which GACAR Part?
questions.explain: GACAR §121.1 ties Part 121 operations to holding an Air Operator Certificate under GACAR Part 119; a certificate holder is defined as a Part 119 AOC holder operating under this part.

questions.q: For the purposes of GACAR Part 121, the term 'special unscheduled' distinguishes requirements applicable to aircraft with a type-certificated passenger seating capacity of —
questions.explain: GACAR §121.5 uses 'special unscheduled' for unscheduled operations applicable only to aircraft with a type-certificated passenger seating capacity of 56 seats or less, excluding required crew members.

questions.q: For scheduled and unscheduled operations, which of the following is NOT one of the full-time management positions a Part 121 certificate holder must staff?
questions.explain: GACAR §121.45(a) requires a director of safety, director of operations, chief pilot, director of maintenance, and chief inspector; a director of training is not among the listed required positions.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.45, a certificate holder must notify the President of any change in required management personnel or any vacancy within how many working days?
questions.explain: GACAR §121.45(f)(3) requires the certificate holder to notify the President within 10 working days of any change in personnel or any vacancy in a listed position.

questions.q: A certificate holder conducting only special unscheduled operations must staff which management positions under GACAR §121.45?
options: Director of operations, chief pilot, and director of maintenance
Director of safety and chief inspector only
Chief pilot and chief inspector only
All five positions required for scheduled operations
questions.explain: GACAR §121.45(b) requires special unscheduled operators to have a director of operations, a chief pilot, and a director of maintenance — a reduced set compared with scheduled operations.

questions.q: To serve as director of operations for a Part 121 certificate holder, a person must hold at minimum which pilot certificate?
questions.explain: GACAR §121.49(a) requires the director of operations to hold an airline transport pilot (ATP) certificate, plus specified supervisory and PIC experience.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.49, to serve as chief inspector a person must hold a mechanic certificate with both airframe and powerplant ratings and have held those ratings for at least —
questions.explain: GACAR §121.49(d) requires the chief inspector to hold a mechanic certificate with airframe and powerplant ratings and to have held those ratings for at least 3 years.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.13, if a certificate holder knowingly permits an owned or leased aircraft to be engaged in an operation violating the psychoactive-substances rule, that operation is a basis for —
questions.explain: GACAR §121.13 provides that permitting an aircraft to be used in violation of GACAR §91.23 (carriage of psychoactive substances) is a basis for suspending or revoking the certificate.

questions.q: Beyond the general Part 91 documents, GACAR §121.17 requires a Part 121 certificate holder to carry on board —
options: A true copy of the AOC and a copy of the operations specifications
A copy of the certificate holder's financial statements
The original AOC and original operations specifications only
questions.explain: GACAR §121.17 requires carrying a true copy of the AOC and a copy of the operations specifications (and, when applicable, a true copy of the Article 83bis agreement).

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.139, each Part 121 certificate holder must prepare and keep current which manuals?
options: An operations manual and a maintenance manual
A marketing manual and a safety manual
questions.explain: GACAR §121.139(a) requires the certificate holder to prepare and keep current both an operations manual and a maintenance manual for the use and guidance of appropriate personnel.

questions.q: Among the requirements of GACAR §121.139, each required manual must —
options: Be available in the English language
Be revised no more than once per year
questions.explain: GACAR §121.139(c) requires each manual to be available in the English language, be easy to revise, reference applicable GACAR, and include human factors principles.

questions.q: GACAR §121.143 lists the content areas that the operations manual must contain. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explain: GACAR §121.143(a) organizes operations-manual contents under General; Aircraft operating information; Areas, routes, and aerodromes; and Training — revenue accounting is not a required content area.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.147, a certificate holder must keep a current approved Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM), or approved equivalent, for each type of aircraft —
options: At its principal base of operations and in each aircraft of that type
Only in the certificate holder's legal department
Only aboard the aircraft during international flights
questions.explain: GACAR §121.147(a) requires a current approved AFM or approved equivalent at the principal base of operations and in each aircraft of that type that the holder operates.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.151, copies of the required manual (or appropriate parts) must be furnished to all of the following EXCEPT —
options: Appropriate ground operations and maintenance personnel
The GACA representatives assigned to it
questions.explain: GACAR §121.151(a) requires furnishing manuals to ground operations and maintenance personnel, crew members, and assigned GACA representatives; passengers are not on that list.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.517, no person may take off an aircraft with inoperable instruments or equipment installed unless —
options: The PIC gives verbal approval before departure
An approved minimum equipment list (MEL) exists and the operations specifications authorize operations under it
The item is scheduled for repair within 10 days
A passenger briefing on the defect is given
questions.explain: GACAR §121.517(a) permits takeoff with inoperable items only when an approved MEL exists and the operations specifications authorize operation under that MEL, with the aircraft operated under its conditions and limitations.

questions.q: Which of the following may NOT be included in a certificate holder's approved MEL under GACAR §121.517?
options: Instruments or equipment required by an airworthiness directive to be operable
questions.explain: GACAR §121.517(b) bars the MEL from including instruments/equipment required by an airworthiness directive to be operable, items required by the type-certification airworthiness requirements, and items required for specific operations by Part 121 and Part 91.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1301, a certificate holder conducting scheduled operations must have which operational-control system?
questions.explain: GACAR §121.1301 requires scheduled operators to have a dispatch release system; unscheduled operators may use either a flight release system or a dispatch release system.

questions.q: Under the dispatch release system of GACAR §121.1309, no person may continue a flight from an intermediate aerodrome without re-dispatch if the aircraft has been on the ground more than —
questions.explain: GACAR §121.1309(a) prohibits continuing a flight from an intermediate aerodrome without re-dispatch once the aircraft has been on the ground more than 6 hours.

questions.q: Under the dispatch release system of GACAR §121.1309, who are jointly responsible for the preflight planning, delay, and dispatch release of a flight?
options: The PIC and the aircraft dispatcher
The chief pilot and the director of safety
The GACA and the certificate holder
The first officer and the cabin crew
questions.explain: GACAR §121.1309(a)(4) makes the PIC and the aircraft dispatcher jointly responsible for the preflight planning, delay, and dispatch release, in compliance with Part 121, the operations specifications, and the manual.

questions.q: Under the flight release system of GACAR §121.1325, operational control for each flight must be shared between the PIC and —
questions.explain: GACAR §121.1325(a) requires operational control for each flight to be shared between the PIC and the director of operations, who may delegate that authority as specified in the manual.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1001, a Part 121 certificate holder may satisfy flight-crew flight-time and duty limitations either by complying with GACAR Part 117 or by implementing —
options: A fatigue risk management system (FRMS) providing an equivalent level of safety
A doubled minimum rest period only
No alternative — Part 117 is the sole option
questions.explain: GACAR §121.1001 lets a certificate holder either comply with the Part 117 flight-time and duty limitations or implement a comprehensive FRMS, approved by the President, that provides an equivalent level of safety.

questions.q: Under an air carrier's operational control, the release of a flight is the joint responsibility of —
options: The pilot in command and (for dispatch operations) the aircraft dispatcher
questions.explain: In dispatch operations, operational control and the flight release are shared between the PIC and the licensed aircraft dispatcher.

questions.q: A Minimum Equipment List (MEL) allows an aircraft to be dispatched with —
options: Specific inoperative items under defined conditions and procedures
questions.explain: An approved MEL permits dispatch with certain items inoperative provided the associated conditions, limitations and procedures are met.

questions.q: Air carrier operations require crew members to complete —
options: Approved training and qualification/checking programs before serving
questions.explain: Part 121/135 carriers must run approved training, qualification and recurrent checking programs; crew must be current and qualified to serve.

questions.q: Flight and duty time limitations for air-carrier crews exist primarily to —
options: Manage fatigue and preserve alertness for safety
questions.explain: Flight, duty and rest limits are safety rules that manage crew fatigue and protect alertness.

questions.q: Scheduled airline operations with transport-category aircraft are governed by GACAR —
questions.explain: Part 121 governs commercial air operators using transport-category/commuter aircraft.

questions.q: Dispatch of a Part 121 flight requires the joint responsibility of —
options: The PIC and the aircraft dispatcher (flight operations officer)
questions.explain: Under Part 121 domestic/flag rules, operational control is shared by the PIC and a licensed dispatcher.

questions.q: A required document carried on a commercial transport flight is the —
options: Operations specifications / operating certificate references and required manuals
questions.explain: Required manuals and operational documents (as specified in the rules and OpSpecs) must be available on board.

questions.q: Extended-range operations (EDTO/ETOPS) impose requirements based on —
options: The diversion time to an adequate aerodrome with an engine inoperative
questions.explain: EDTO/ETOPS rules apply additional requirements tied to the maximum diversion time to a suitable aerodrome.

questions.q: A cabin crew complement on a transport aircraft is determined mainly by —
questions.explain: The minimum number of cabin crew is set by the passenger seating capacity (and type certification).

questions.q: Fuel requirements for a Part 121 flight include trip fuel, contingency, alternate and —
questions.explain: Transport fuel planning adds final reserve/holding fuel on top of trip, contingency and alternate requirements.

questions.q: Flight-time and duty limitations for airline crews are intended to —
questions.explain: Flight/duty/rest limits manage crew fatigue in scheduled operations.

questions.q: A required element of a Part 121 operator's programme is —
options: An approved training and checking programme for crews
questions.explain: Approved training/checking programmes for flight and cabin crew are required.

questions.q: The aircraft used in Part 121 operations must be maintained under —
questions.explain: Part 121 fleets follow a continuous airworthiness maintenance programme.

questions.q: A minimum equipment list (MEL) allows a transport aircraft to be dispatched —
options: With certain items inoperative under defined conditions
questions.explain: An approved MEL permits dispatch with specified inoperative items subject to operational/maintenance conditions.

questions.q: Weather minima for dispatch consider the destination and —
questions.explain: Dispatch requires take-off, destination and (where required) alternate minima to be satisfied by the forecast.

questions.q: A load and trim (weight-and-balance) sheet for a transport flight ensures the aircraft is —
options: Within weight and CG limits for the flight
questions.explain: The load sheet confirms take-off/landing weights and CG are within the certified envelope.

banks.title: Transport Performance & Dispatch
banks.desc: Performance, weather minima and dispatch requirements for transport-category operations (GACAR Part 121).
banks.source: GACAR Part 121 (performance & dispatch) · DRAFT — pending review

questions.q: Which subpart of GACAR Part 121 prescribes airplane performance operating limitations for all certificate holders?
questions.explain: Subpart F prescribes airplane performance operating limitations; Subpart G covers rotorcraft performance, Subpart M covers dispatcher qualifications, and Subpart Q covers records and reports.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.263, in computing takeoff distance the length of any clearway that may be included must not be greater than —
options: One-quarter the length of the runway
One-half the length of the runway
The full length of the runway
One-and-a-half times the length of the runway
questions.explain: §121.263 provides that the takeoff distance must not exceed the runway plus any clearway, but the clearway credited must not be greater than one-half the length of the runway.

questions.q: Under the destination landing limitations of GACAR §121.275, a turbojet-powered airplane's mass at takeoff must allow a full-stop landing within what portion of the effective runway length at the destination?
questions.explain: §121.275 requires that the anticipated landing mass allow a full-stop landing within 60 percent of the effective length of the runway (measured from 50 ft above the runway) for turbojet airplanes at the destination.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.275, if weather reports indicate the destination runways may be wet or slippery, a turbojet airplane may take off only if the effective runway length is at least what percentage of the dry-runway length otherwise required?
questions.explain: §121.275 requires that, for wet or slippery destination runways, the effective runway length be at least 115 percent of the length required for dry conditions, unless a shorter approved wet distance is in the AFM.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.279, an aerodrome may be listed as an alternate for a turbopropeller-powered airplane only if the aircraft can be brought to a full stop within what portion of the effective runway length?
questions.explain: §121.279 permits listing an alternate for a turbopropeller airplane only if a full-stop landing can be made within 70 percent of the effective runway length (60 percent for turbojet airplanes).

questions.q: GACAR §121.271 (en-route limitations, two engines inoperative) allows compliance by ensuring no point along the intended track is more than how long — with all engines operating at cruising power — from an adequate aerodrome?
questions.explain: One compliance option in §121.271 is that no place along the intended track is more than 90 minutes (all engines at cruising power) from an aerodrome meeting §121.279.

questions.q: Under the en-route limitation for one engine inoperative (GACAR §121.267), the airplane's mass must permit a net flight path clearing terrain and obstructions within the specified corridor by at least —
questions.explain: §121.267 requires (for the option reaching a landing aerodrome) that the one-engine-inoperative net flight path clear all terrain and obstructions within 4.4 NM of track by at least 2,000 ft vertically.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1309, no flight under the dispatch release system may start unless —
options: The pilot-in-command alone signs the load manifest
An aircraft dispatcher specifically authorizes that flight
The airplane has departed within the previous hour
questions.explain: §121.1309 provides that no person may start a flight unless an aircraft dispatcher specifically authorizes it, and the PIC and dispatcher are jointly responsible for preflight planning and dispatch release.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1309, a flight may not continue from an intermediate aerodrome without a re-dispatch if the aircraft has been on the ground more than —
questions.explain: §121.1309 requires re-dispatch to continue a flight from an intermediate aerodrome when the aircraft has been on the ground more than 6 hours.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1369, an aircraft may be dispatched or released for operations under IFR or over-the-top only when appropriate weather reports or forecasts indicate that the weather at the destination will be —
options: At or above the authorized minimums at the estimated time of arrival
VFR at all times en route
questions.explain: §121.1369 permits IFR/over-the-top dispatch or release only when weather reports or forecasts indicate conditions will be at or above the authorized minimums at the estimated time of arrival at the destination.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1393, a flight conducted under IFR or over-the-top must generally have how many destination alternate aerodromes specified in the dispatch or flight release?
options: None if the flight is under 3 hours
One alternate only for extended over-water flights
questions.explain: §121.1393 requires at least one destination alternate aerodrome be selected and specified for IFR or over-the-top flights, subject to limited exceptions (e.g., favorable forecast ceiling/visibility windows or isolated aerodromes).

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1397, no aerodrome may be listed as an alternate in a dispatch or flight release unless the appropriate weather reports or forecasts indicate the weather will be —
options: At or above the alternate weather minimums in the operations specifications when the flight arrives
Below landing minimums but with an ILS available
questions.explain: §121.1397 permits listing an alternate only when the weather is forecast to be at or above the alternate weather minimums in the certificate holder's operations specifications at the time the flight arrives.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1389, when a takeoff alternate is required, for an airplane having two engines the takeoff alternate must be located no more than —
options: 1 hour from the departure aerodrome at one-engine-inoperative cruise speed
2 hours from the departure aerodrome at all-engine cruise speed
questions.explain: §121.1389 requires a two-engine airplane's takeoff alternate to be within 1 hour of the departure aerodrome at the normal one-engine-inoperative cruising speed (ISA, still air, actual takeoff mass); three-or-more-engine airplanes get 2 hours at all-engine cruise.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1365, an aircraft may be dispatched or released for VFR operation only if the ceiling and visibility en route —
options: Are forecast to improve after departure
Are and will remain at or above applicable VFR minimums until arrival at the specified aerodrome(s)
Are reported at the departure aerodrome only
questions.explain: §121.1365 permits VFR dispatch or release only when weather reports or forecasts show the ceiling and visibility en route are and will remain at or above applicable VFR minimums until the aircraft reaches the aerodrome(s) specified.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1349, before releasing (or beginning) a flight, the aircraft dispatcher or PIC must —
options: Be thoroughly familiar with reported and forecast weather conditions on the route to be flown
File a written risk assessment with the President
questions.explain: §121.1349 requires the aircraft dispatcher (dispatch release system) or the PIC (flight release system) to be thoroughly familiar with reported and forecast weather conditions on the route to be flown before releasing/beginning the flight.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1341, a flight may not be allowed to continue to the aerodrome to which it was released unless the weather at a specified alternate is forecast to be —
options: At or above the alternate minimums in the operations specifications at the time the aircraft would arrive there
Clear of clouds regardless of visibility
The same as the departure aerodrome
questions.explain: §121.1341 prohibits continuing a flight unless the weather at a specified alternate is forecast to be at or above the alternate minimums in the operations specifications when the aircraft would arrive; the release may be amended en route to add an alternate within fuel range.

questions.q: GACAR §121.89 addresses ETOPS communications facilities. What does it primarily require of the certificate holder?
options: Provide voice communications for ETOPS where such facilities are available, considering diversion routes and altitudes
Install a second HF radio in every airplane
Restrict ETOPS to daylight hours only
Carry a satellite phone for each passenger
questions.explain: §121.89 requires the certificate holder to provide voice communications for ETOPS where facilities are available, considering potential routes and altitudes needed for diversion to ETOPS alternate aerodromes, substituting an approved system where voice is not possible.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1401, an aircraft may be dispatched or released for an ETOPS flight only if —
options: The destination weather is forecast VFR
Enough ETOPS alternate aerodromes are listed so the aircraft remains within the authorized ETOPS maximum diversion time
Every alternate has a precision approach
questions.explain: §121.1401 requires that enough ETOPS alternate aerodromes be listed in the dispatch or flight release so the aircraft remains within the authorized ETOPS maximum diversion time, selecting from adequate aerodromes meeting the standards of the part.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1409, for ETOPS up to and including 180 minutes, an aerodrome may not be listed as an ETOPS alternate if the time needed to reach it exceeds the aircraft's most limiting ETOPS significant system time minus —
questions.explain: §121.1409 provides that, for ETOPS up to 180 minutes, an aerodrome cannot be an ETOPS alternate if the flight time to it (one-engine-inoperative cruise, standard conditions) exceeds the most limiting ETOPS significant system time minus 15 minutes.

questions.q: Under the ETOPS fuel-supply rule (GACAR §121.1417), the aircraft must carry fuel to hold at 1,500 ft above field elevation upon reaching an ETOPS alternate for how long, then conduct an approach and land?
questions.explain: §121.1417 requires ETOPS fuel sufficient to hold at 1,500 ft above field elevation for 15 minutes upon reaching an ETOPS alternate aerodrome and then conduct an instrument approach and land, in addition to diversion, wind, icing, and deterioration allowances.

questions.q: Under GACAR §121.1417, when calculating ETOPS diversion fuel the certificate holder must increase the forecast wind speed by what margin to account for wind-forecasting errors?
questions.explain: §121.1417 requires the actual forecast wind speed to be increased by 5 percent (increasing headwind or decreasing tailwind) — or additional reserve fuel equal to 5 percent of the diversion fuel — to account for potential wind-forecasting errors.

questions.q: For a transport-category take-off, V1 is the —
options: Take-off decision speed — the maximum speed at which the pilot must take the first action to stop within the accelerate-stop distance
questions.explain: V1 is the decision speed: at or below it the take-off can be safely rejected within the accelerate-stop distance; above it the take-off is continued.

questions.q: The 'balanced field length' is the runway length at which —
options: The accelerate-stop distance equals the accelerate-go distance for the chosen V1
questions.explain: At the balanced field length the distance to accelerate to V1 and stop equals the distance to accelerate to V1, lose an engine, and continue to the screen height.

questions.q: Following an engine failure at altitude on a transport aircraft, 'driftdown' refers to —
options: A controlled descent to the one-engine-inoperative net level-off altitude while maintaining obstacle clearance
questions.explain: Driftdown is the planned descent on the remaining engine(s) to the OEI net ceiling, ensuring the net flight path clears enroute obstacles/terrain.

questions.q: Transport-category landing performance requires the aeroplane to be able to land within —
options: A defined percentage of the landing distance available (a required landing factor)
questions.explain: Dispatch landing performance requires the aeroplane to stop within a required proportion of the landing distance available (a safety factor applied to the demonstrated landing distance).

questions.q: Performance Class A (transport) aeroplanes must be able to continue a take-off safely after —
options: A critical engine failure at or after V1
questions.explain: Class A performance guarantees a take-off can be continued (or safely rejected) around the V1 decision speed with the critical engine failed.

questions.q: The net take-off flight path is the gross flight path reduced by a margin to —
questions.explain: The net flight path applies a safety decrement to the demonstrated (gross) climb to ensure obstacle clearance after take-off.

questions.q: Contaminated-runway take-off performance accounts for —
options: Reduced braking and possible impingement/displacement drag
questions.explain: Standing water/slush/snow reduce braking and add drag, degrading accelerate-stop and continued take-off performance.

questions.q: Wind-shear on approach is most dangerous because it can cause a rapid loss of —
options: Airspeed and lift close to the ground
questions.explain: A shift from headwind to tailwind (or a downdraft) can rob the aircraft of airspeed and lift at low altitude — hence wind-shear escape procedures.

questions.q: A cost-index setting in an FMS balances —
options: Fuel cost against time-related cost to derive an economy speed
questions.explain: The cost index trades fuel burn against time-dependent costs to compute the economical climb/cruise/descent speeds.

questions.q: Jet-stream cores are associated with —
options: Strong winds and clear-air turbulence at their boundaries
questions.explain: Jet streams bring very strong winds and CAT, especially on the cold (polar) side and near the tropopause breaks.

questions.q: A tropopause height that is lower generally indicates —
questions.explain: The tropopause is lower over the poles (colder) and higher over the tropics (warmer) — relevant to cruise levels and jet streams.

questions.q: A significant weather (SIGWX) chart depicts —
options: Fronts, jet streams, CAT, cloud and hazards for the cruise levels
questions.explain: SIGWX charts show significant en-route weather — fronts, jets, turbulence, icing, cloud and convection — for flight planning.

questions.q: The maximum operating limit speed by Mach number for a transport jet is —
questions.explain: MMO is the maximum operating Mach number; VMO is the maximum operating airspeed — both must not be exceeded.

questions.q: High-altitude 'coffin corner' is the narrowing gap between —
questions.explain: Near the service ceiling the stall speed and the critical Mach converge, shrinking the safe speed range ('coffin corner').

questions.q: Reduced-thrust (flex) take-offs are permitted only when —
options: Actual performance requirements are still met with margin
questions.explain: Flex/derated thrust is used only when the reduced thrust still satisfies field, climb and obstacle requirements.

questions.q: An accurate outside air temperature is important at altitude because it affects —
options: True airspeed, Mach and performance calculations
questions.explain: OAT feeds TAS/Mach computation and performance; errors affect navigation timing and buffet margins.

questions.q: A standard alternate-fuel requirement for a transport flight is based on —
options: The distance/time to the alternate plus approach and landing
questions.explain: Alternate fuel covers the missed approach at destination, cruise to the alternate, approach and landing there.
